title: Rhythm and Meter
intro: Rhythm is how sounds are placed in time. Notation writes durations as fractions of a whole note; meter groups the steady beat into strong and weak pulses. This chapter covers note values first, then meter, then the ways music plays against the beat.

blocks.text: Most music has a steady pulse you can tap your foot to: the beat. Its speed is the tempo, in beats per minute (BPM). A slow ballad might be 60–70 BPM, a march about 120, fast bebop 250 or more. Italian tempo words give the same information loosely: largo (very slow), adagio, andante (walking pace), moderato, allegro (fast), presto (very fast).
Durations are written as fractions of a whole note. Each value is half the one before:

items: Whole note 𝅝 = 4 quarter notes (an open note head, no stem).
Half note 𝅗𝅥 = 2 quarter notes (open head with a stem).
Quarter note ♩ = 1 beat in most meters (filled head with a stem).
Eighth note ♪ = ½ quarter (one flag, or beamed in groups).
Sixteenth note = ¼ quarter (two flags or beams); thirty-second = ⅛ (three).
Each value has a matching rest of the same length, a silence.

blocks.text: A dot after a note adds half its value: a dotted half note is 2 + 1 = 3 beats, a dotted quarter 1 + ½ = 1½. A second dot adds a quarter more. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound, which lets a note last across a bar line.

blocks.title: Add it up
blocks.text: How many quarter-note beats last: a dotted half note tied to an eighth note?
solution: Dotted half = 2 + 1 = 3 beats; eighth = ½ beat; tied together = 3½ beats.

blocks.title: Tempo
blocks.text: At 90 BPM, how long in seconds is a dotted quarter note?
solution: One beat lasts 60/90 = 0.667 s; a dotted quarter is 1.5 beats = 1.0 s.

blocks.text: Sources: Gould, E. (2011). Behind Bars: The Definitive Guide to Music Notation. Faber Music; London, J. (2012). Hearing in Time, 2nd ed. Oxford University Press; Kostka, S., Payne, D. & Almén, B. (2018). Tonal Harmony, 8th ed. McGraw-Hill.
